data.title: Macular and lichen amyloidosis — viva
data.summary: Nutritional & metabolic · 15 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Macular and lichen amyloidosis** (Nutritional & metabolic)_

**Q1. What is amyloidosis? Classify cutaneous amyloidosis.**
- Extracellular deposition of insoluble fibrillar proteins with β-pleated sheet structure that show apple-green birefringence with Congo red
- Primary localised cutaneous amyloidosis (PLCA): keratinocyte-derived (amyloid K) — macular, lichen (papular), biphasic (both), nodular (AL — plasma-cell light chains; risk of systemic progression ~7%), poikiloderma-like, bullous, anosacral, familial (OSMR, IL31RA mutations)
- Secondary localised: in tumours (BCC, seborrhoeic keratosis), PUVA, after injections (insulin amyloid)
- Systemic amyloidosis with skin involvement: AL (primary/myeloma — periorbital 'pinch purpura', waxy papules, macroglossia), AA (secondary — chronic inflammation; skin rarely involved), β2-microglobulin (dialysis), ATTR (familial/senile)

**Q2. Describe macular amyloidosis.**
- Grey-brown rippled (reticulate) pigmentation on the upper back (interscapular), arms, shins; mild to moderate itch
- Common in Asians, Middle East, Latin Americans; women; friction (nylon scrubs, loofahs, towels — 'friction melanosis' overlap)

**Q3. Describe lichen amyloidosis.**
- Very itchy, discrete firm hyperkeratotic hyperpigmented papules often in a rippled/linear pattern coalescing into plaques on shins (commonest), extensor forearms, thighs, upper back; men > women
- Associations: atopic dermatitis, MEN 2A (RET), familial (OSMR/IL31RA), chronic friction/scratching, lichen planus, hepatitis/biliary cirrhosis

**Q4. Pathogenesis.**
- Keratinocyte damage (friction, scratching, UV, genetic) → apoptotic keratinocyte filaments (cytokeratins, especially CK5) altered into amyloid by dermal macrophages/fibroblasts → deposits in papillary dermis
- Itch–scratch cycle perpetuates (IL-31/OSMR pathway)

**Q5. Describe stains used for amyloid (PYQ).**
- Congo red — salmon pink on light microscopy; apple-green birefringence under polarised light (gold standard)
- Crystal violet / methyl violet — metachromasia (purple-red)
- Thioflavin T / S — yellow-green fluorescence under UV (sensitive)
- Sirius red, PAS (weakly positive, diastase resistant), Alcian blue, Pagoda red, DFF (dylon), cotton dyes (Pagoda red, Dylon) — high sensitivity in skin
- Immunohistochemistry: anti-cytokeratin (34βE12 — PLCA), anti-κ/λ (AL), anti-AA, anti-TTR
- Electron microscopy: non-branching 7.5–10 nm fibrils
- Lugol's iodine (gross specimen — mahogany brown, turning blue with sulphuric acid)

**Q6. Histopathology of macular/lichen amyloidosis.**
- Small globular eosinophilic deposits in dermal papillae (macular — subtle, needs special stains), with pigment incontinence (melanophages)
- Lichen: larger deposits filling and expanding papillae + hyperkeratosis, acanthosis (features of chronic rubbing)
- Nodular: diffuse deposits throughout dermis, around vessels, with plasma cells (AL type)

**Q7. Differential diagnosis.**
- Macular: post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, notalgia paraesthetica (localised itchy patch under scapula — T2–T6 nerve entrapment), friction melanosis, ashy dermatosis, lichen planus pigmentosus, prurigo pigmentosa, confluent and reticulated papillomatosis, tinea versicolor
- Lichen: lichen simplex chronicus, hypertrophic LP, prurigo nodularis, pretibial myxoedema, colloid milium, lichen myxoedematosus

**Q8. Investigations.**
- Clinical + dermoscopy (central white/brown hub with radiating pigmentation); biopsy with special stains
- If nodular amyloidosis or systemic signs: serum and urine protein electrophoresis, immunofixation, serum free light chains, CBC, renal function, urine protein, echocardiography, abdominal fat-pad aspirate; MEN 2A screening (calcitonin, metanephrines, RET) in familial lichen amyloidosis with family history of medullary thyroid cancer

**Q9. Management.**
- Avoid friction (no nylon scrubbers), break itch–scratch cycle, sedating antihistamines, emollients, menthol/pramoxine
- Potent topical steroids under occlusion, intralesional triamcinolone (lichen), tacrolimus, calcipotriol, DMSO (dimethyl sulphoxide), capsaicin
- Keratolytics (salicylic acid, urea) for lichen papules; acitretin 0.5 mg/kg/day for extensive lichen amyloidosis
- Phototherapy (NB-UVB, PUVA), cyclosporine, dupilumab/nemolizumab (itch — case reports)
- Procedures: dermabrasion, CO2/Er:YAG laser, Q-switched Nd:YAG (macular pigment), fractional lasers
- Nodular: excision, laser; follow up for systemic AL

**Q10. Prognosis.**
- Benign chronic course; recurrence common; nodular type needs monitoring for systemic amyloidosis

**Q11. What is nodular amyloidosis and why follow up?**
- Single or multiple waxy yellow-pink nodules/ plaques on face, legs, genitals; AL (light-chain) amyloid from local plasma cell clone; ~7% progress to systemic AL amyloidosis or are associated with Sjögren's — need SPEP/ immunofixation and annual review

**Q12. Systemic AL amyloidosis skin signs.**
- Pinch purpura (periorbital 'raccoon eyes' after coughing/ proctoscopy), waxy translucent papules (eyelids, flexures), macroglossia, nail dystrophy, alopecia, scleroderma-like induration, carpal tunnel syndrome; heart/ kidney involvement determines prognosis

**Q13. What is biphasic amyloidosis?**
- Coexistence of macular and lichen amyloidosis in the same patient — supports the view that they are a spectrum of the same keratinocyte-derived process

**Q14. Friction melanosis vs macular amyloidosis.**
- Friction melanosis: dark pigmentation over bony prominences (clavicles, scapulae, spine) from nylon towels/ scrubbers, no amyloid on special stains; macular amyloidosis: rippled pigmentation with amyloid deposits — both improved by stopping friction

**Q15. What is notalgia paraesthetica?**
- Localised itchy, sometimes burning hyperpigmented patch medial to the scapula (T2–T6) due to dorsal spinal nerve entrapment/ degenerative spine disease; may show secondary macular amyloid; treat with capsaicin, lidocaine, gabapentin, physiotherapy, botulinum toxin

## Quick spotter facts
- Rippled grey-brown interscapular pigmentation — macular amyloidosis
- Itchy rippled papules on shins — lichen amyloidosis
- Congo red apple-green birefringence

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Cutaneous amyloidosis). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
